title: The combined action of suicide gene exosomes from pancreatic cancer-associated fibroblasts and from mesenchymal stem cells as a pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma treatment approach
projectDescription: Exosomes from pancreatic cancer-associated fibroblasts and mesenchymal stem cells that have been transduced with the yeast cytosine deaminase::uracil phosphoribosyl transferase release suicide gene exosomes acting as "Trojan horse" drugs, effectively killing pancreatic cancer cells by converting the non-toxic prodrug 5-fluorocytosine intracellularly into the cytotoxic 5-fluorouracil. We have shown in experiments in vitro, involving a simulated desmoplastic pancreatic tumor, that the combined action of these targeted exosomes could be an approach for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma treatment.
sampleProcessingProtocol: From the resected tumor tissue, a specimen for histopathological examination was taken, and the rest of the tissue was fragmented into small pieces, suspended in a freezing medium, and stored in a liquid nitrogen biobank. To isolate the PCAFs, tumor tissue fragments were adhered to a plastic tissue culture dish and surrounded with a complete culture medium (Gibco low glucose DMEM) supplemented with 5% PL. The next day, the fragments were overlaid with medium and cultivated at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO2. Two to three days later, the PCAFs began to migrate from the adhered tumor tissue explants. When the dish of PCAFs was near the confluence, the fragments were transferred to a new dish. Up to 20 transfers of tumor stroma specimens were realized with continued PCAF production. The same technique was used to isolate fibroblasts from human omentum tissue. To prepare PCAFs expressing the yCD::UPRT gene from retrovirus integrated into cell DNA, the sub-confluent cells were infected with replication-defective retrovirus with mixed amphotropic and ecotropic envelope glycoproteins. The multiplicity of infection of tumor cells was 10 infectious units per cell. Virus-infected PCAFs were cultivated in selection media containing a pretested concentration of G418 (0.5-1.2 mg/mL of G418) to obtain a homogenous population of yCD::UPRT gene-transduced PCAFs – the addition of 5-FC to such cells induced apoptotic death.   The source of exosomes was a 24-hour CM free of growth supplements collected from 80% confluent cell cultures of 98% cell viability as assessed by Trypan-Blue exclusion (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO). CM was centrifuged at 800g for 5 minutes, and filtered through a 0.22μm syringe filter to remove debris. Exosomes from CM were concentrated via various techniques, such as TFF-Easy cartridge, and membrane affinity spin columns, using exoEasy Maxi Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany), or by size-exclusion chromatography. The exosomes were purified and concentrated by TFF-Easy tangential flow filtration-based device with 5 nM cut-off holes (HansaBioMed Life Sciences Ltd. Tallinn, Estonia).  Proteins from exosomes were extracted in SDT buffer (4% SDS, 0.1M DTT, 0.1M Tris/HCl, pH 7.6) in a thermomixer (Eppendorf ThermoMixer C, 60 min, 95°C, 750 rpm). After that, all samples were centrifuged (15 min, 20,000 x g) and the supernatants (ca 25 μg of total protein) were used for filter-aided sample preparation (FASP) as described elsewhere (Wisniewski et. all, 2009) using 1 μg of trypsin (sequencing grade; Promega). The resulting peptides were extracted into LC-MS vials by 2.5% formic acid (FA) in 50% acetonitrile (ACN) and 100% ACN with the addition of polyethylene glycol (final concentration 0.001%) and concentrated in a SpeedVac concentrator (Thermo Fisher Scientific). LC-MS/MS analyses of all peptides were done using UltiMate 3000 RSLCnano system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) connected to timsTOF Pro mass spectrometer (Bruker). Before LC separation, tryptic digests were online concentrated and desalted using a trapping column (Acclaim PepMap 100 C18, dimensions 300 μm ID, 5 mm long, 5 μm particles, Thermo Fisher Scientific). The trap column was then washed with 0.1% TFA and the peptides were eluted in backflush mode from the trapping column onto an analytical column (Aurora C18, 75μm ID, 250 mm long, 1.6 μm particles, Ion Opticks) by 90 min gradient program (flow rate 300 nl.min-1, 3-42% of mobile phase B; mobile phase A: 0.1% FA in water; mobile phase B: 0.1% FA in 80% ACN) followed by 10 min long system wash using 80% of mobile phase B. Equilibration of the trapping column and the analytical column was done before sample injection to sample loop. The analytical column was installed in the Captive Spray ion source (Bruker; temperatures set to 50 ºC) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Spray voltage and sheath gas were set to 1.5kV and 1, respectively.  MSn data were acquired in data-independent acquisition (DIA) mode with base method m/z range of 100-1700 and 1/k0 range of 0.6-1.4 V×s×cm-2. Enclosed DIAparameters.txt file defined m/z 400-1000 precursor range with equal windows size of 21 Th using two steps for each PASEF scan and cycle time of 100ms locked to 100% duty cycle.
dataProcessingProtocol: DIA data were processed in DIA-NN (version 1.8.1, Demichev et all., 2020) in library-free mode against the modified cRAP database (based on http://www.thegpm.org/crap; 111 sequences in total, version 2018/11), the UniProtKB protein database for Homo sapiens (https://www.uniprot.org/proteomes/UP000005640); version 2023/09, number of protein sequences: 20,594) and sequences of two yeast proteins (UniProt accessions Q12178 and P18562). No optional, but carbamidomethylation as fixed modification and trypsin/P enzyme with 1 allowed missed cleavages and peptide length 7-30 were set during the library preparation. False discovery rate (FDR) control was set to 1% FDR. MS1 and MS2 accuracies as well as scan window parameters were set based on the initial test searches (median value from all samples ascertained parameter values). MBR was switched on. Protein MaxLFQ intensities reported in the DIA-NN main report file were further processed using the software container environment (https://github.com/OmicsWorkflows), version 4.7.7a. Processing workflow is available upon request . Briefly, it covered: a) removal of low-quality precursors and contaminant protein groups, b) protein group MaxLFQ intensities log2 transformation, c) filtering out of protein groups not quantified in more than 80 % of the replicates of at least one sample type, d) imputation of the missing values from the random distribution around the global minimal value, e) differential expression analysis using LIMMA statistical test – proteins with adjusted p-value <0.05 and fold change >2 were considered as significantly changing ones  f) protein abundance in ppm calculation.
